newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE ENJOYING LOVE AFFAIR WITH U.S. OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE ENJOYING LOVE AFFAIR WITH U.S. OPEN.

text.p: It is the major that Colin Montgomerie loves most, the major whose tradition and supreme test of golf skills ranks it as most important to the burly Scotsman.
Surprisingly, it is not the British Open, which is being played next month at Royal Troon, where Montgomerie's father serves as club secretary.
It is the U.S. Open.
"I love it here," Montgomerie said after walking the straight and narrow through Congressional's rough-bordered fairways to post a tournament-leading 65.
"I'm as happy playing in the U.S. Open as Tiger Woods is playing the Masters. This is a tournament where I'm very, very comfortable. I look forward to any round I play and any shot I hit."
Most golfers would view a round at the U.S. Open as a masochist's delight. Narrow fairways, ball-swallowing rough, 480-yard par-4s, water hazards and even snakes slithering by the 18th green.
But all this is what makes Montgomerie's heart sing.
"I tend to drive the ball straight as anybody," the 33-year-old European Ryder Cup star said after his five-under round. And that is a great advantage here.
"And my iron shots off good lies are usually quite good," added Montomerie in typically British understatement. His four birdie putts on the back nine were all 15 feet or less.
"So I'm very happy playing U.S. Opens. I just wish there were more tournaments set up this way."
The Briton could not say enough good things about the conditions at Congressional, which Greg Norman affectionately referred to as "a beast" before going out and shooting a first-round 75.
"I have to say this course is as good a conditioned course as you will find anywhere. The way they mow the fairways with the green mowers back and forth is tremendous," he said.
"My caddie went to the course at 6 a.m. to get the pins and there were 30 workers out there mowing the fairways. All credit to them for enabling us to have perfect lies to hit good iron shots."
Montgomerie has played great golf in the past at U.S. Opens, but has just missed breaking through for victory and his first major title.

At the 1992 Open at Pebble Beach, he walked off the course looking like the winner until Tom Kite charged to victory. In 1994 he lost in a three-way playoff won by South African Ernie Els. Last year, he tied for 10th at Oakland Hills.
The near-misses have not soured Montgomerie.
"I remember watching Tom Watson at Pebble Beach," Montgomerie said when asked about his first U.S. Open memory.
"That was in the early '80s (1982), I think when he chipped in at 17 and I remember looking at the rough and thinking how difficult that was.
"I just love this course and the tradition of it and the way that the courses are set up."
Montgomerie, who also lost in a playoff against Steve Elkington for the 1995 PGA Championship, would dearly love to win a major -- and win it at a U.S. Open -- but it is not his top priority.

"Golf is very much a job for me. And I have a lovely wife and two lovely daughters," said Montgomerie, who withdrew from a European tour event in Hamburg earlier this year to take care of his daughters when his wife took ill.
"They are one, two and three in my life and golf is very much secondary to that."
Montgomerie, the leading money winner on the European tour for four years running, is focused for now on his quest for one of golf's greatest prizes.
"The British Open, obviously, is something I've looked forward to since it was announced that it was coming to Troon," said Montgomerie.
"But this, to me, is my favourite tournament of the year."
And even with three rounds yet to play here, Montgomerie said: "I look forward to 1998's U.S. Open already."
